File paths cited in answers become links that open a snippet of the file.

End-to-end ML paper workflow with checklists and citation handling.
Market, brand and financial consulting-style research reports.

Watches named companies for material news and produces cited digests.
Reads RSS, Atom and JSON feeds and discovers feeds behind a page.

Source guides and scripts for entity research across public registries and sanctions lists.

Reads subreddits, searches, threads and users without a browser.
Fetches a YouTube transcript and turns it into summaries, threads or posts.
Read-only search across connected chat sources by account, channel, sender, keyword and time, with citations.

Linked git worktrees reuse the main checkout's index and overlay only changed files.

Formulates a search from the task and screen and retrieves how-to knowledge before acting.
Multi-perspective persona generation, outline generation, citation-grounded article writing and a polish pass.
Wide research with many parallel sub-agents
Manus-style wide research that fans one question out to up to 100 parallel sub-agents and merges results.
Enrich and score a prospect set, exclude duplicates, and export the results.
Store probabilistic forecasts and compute a calibration score once outcomes are recorded.

Fly-brain work lives under experiments/ with no AGI, sentience or token-savings claim without a measurement.
Permission modes (Ask, Plan, Auto, Full access / YOLO)
One switch per conversation decides how much the agent may do without asking, from asking about everything to a full-access mode that asks nothing a rule does not cover.
Plan mode (read and propose, never change)
A read-only mode where the agent researches and writes a plan; changes are refused, and leaving plan mode needs the user's approval of the plan.
Every tool call is matched against prioritised allow, ask and deny rules (tool name, argument patterns, shell prefixes, MCP server), from default, user, project and session layers.
Remember 'always allow' as a saved rule
Answering 'always' writes a matching rule (per agent, server or command) so the same request is not asked again, and past approvals can be mined into rule suggestions.
Pick the right command prefix for 'always allow'
When the user always-allows a command, they choose the scope (npm, npm install, npm install lodash) instead of approving the exact string or everything.
Separate switches auto-approve reads, writes (inside or outside the workspace, protected files), commands, MCP tools, mode switches and subtasks, with a quick toggle.
Auto-approval pauses for the user after a set number of model requests or a spend total within a task.
With auto-answer on, a visible countdown picks the suggested answer unless the user types.
Long-running commands are killed after N seconds, except allow-listed ones such as dev servers.
Approval prompt (allow once, always, deny with diff)
An inline approval card shows the exact command or diff and offers allow once, allow always with an editable scope, or deny with feedback; several requests queue.
Edit a proposed change before approving
Before approving an edit, the user opens it in their editor and the edited version is what gets applied.
One approval path for every client (bus and routing)
Approval requests and decisions travel over one channel so the window, CLI, headless runs and sub-agents share the same approval flow, and pending requests drain cleanly.
When the agent waits on an approval, the question is forwarded to the user's chat app with buttons or /approve, and the result is posted back.
Headless runs deny instead of hanging
When nobody can answer an approval (headless or child sessions), the call is denied with an error instead of waiting forever.
Pause a run for approval and resume it
A tool call needing approval suspends the run with an explicit waiting state; approving or declining resumes exactly that run, and pending approvals sit in an inbox.
Every tool call carries a low/medium/high risk level that analyzers can raise, and a policy (always, never, only risky) decides what pauses for approval.
A separate locked-down reviewer model judges flagged or rule-missing calls and allows once, denies with a reason or escalates to the user.
If the reviewer keeps denying or failing, the agent falls back to asking the user, and a denied action can be retried once with the user's explicit yes.
Shell commands are parsed (quotes, nesting, bash -c, PowerShell) and checked against destructive and threat patterns such as rm -rf or curl piped to bash before they run.
A short list of catastrophic commands (recursive delete of the workspace, force push, disk format, sudo password piping) is blocked or always asks, even in full access.
Chained, piped and wrapped commands (&&, pipes, sudo, cmd /c, package-manager exec) are split to the real executables so an approval cannot be widened.
Shell commands are checked against allow and deny lists (longest prefix wins across every chained part), with ask-on-miss and saved allow-always decisions.
Known read-only commands (cat, grep, ls, git status, read-only gh) are recognised and run without a prompt in stricter modes.
Agent cannot damage its own install
Commands that would tamper with the agent's own control state, rewrite its checkout, delete its interpreter or touch its user-data database are refused.
Protected config and instruction files always ask
Edits to the agent's own config, rules and instruction files (and .git) always ask or stay read-only, even under broad allow.
Reads and writes of .env files, ~/.ssh, cloud credentials, the agent's credential files and other profiles' homes are refused or ask, except .env.example.
A gitignore-style file keeps chosen files out of tools and @-mentions.
Workspace boundary for file and shell tools
File and shell access outside the project folder asks or is refused; paths are canonicalised so symlinks cannot sneak out.
When the agent needs a path or network access it lacks, it asks; the user grants it for the session or permanently.
Safe upload, download and served-file paths
Uploaded, downloaded and served files cannot escape their folder through crafted names or traversal.
Writes refuse to follow planted symlinks and use create-exclusive files, so edits cannot land outside their root.
Opening an untrusted folder runs in a safe mode (no project settings, hooks, MCP servers or custom commands) until the user trusts it, after a scan of what it contains.
Re-approve project hooks and policy files when they change
Project hooks and policy files are hashed; new or changed ones need the user's approval before they take effect.
OS sandbox for commands (Seatbelt, bubblewrap, Landlock)
Each shell command runs in a kernel sandbox that limits writes to allowed folders and blocks network unless allowed.
On Windows, commands run under an AppContainer or restricted token with ACLs so the agent cannot reach beyond its folders.
Sandbox modes and named permission profiles
Pick read-only, workspace-write or full access, or named profiles describing folders, globs and network rules that can extend each other.
Run the whole app in a container or sandbox
The whole agent can be relaunched inside Docker, Podman, gVisor or a Seatbelt profile, optionally with an egress firewall.
Sandbox backends (Docker per agent, SSH, remote machines)
Tools run inside a container scoped per agent or session (no network, read-only root, capabilities dropped) or on a remote machine, with a file bridge.
Sessions, processes, disk and run time inside the sandbox are capped, failing closed.
Explain where tools run and why something is blocked
A command explains which sandbox a session's tools use and why an action was blocked.
Scripts that call several tools at once run inside a WebAssembly or V8 isolate.
Static checks on user code blocks
User code blocks are scanned for subprocess/exec-style calls and refused.
Scripts go through the same approval gate
Code sent to an execute-code tool passes the same approval checks as terminal commands.
Network allowlist proxy for sandboxed commands
Sandboxed commands reach the network only through a proxy that allows listed domains and can ask the user about new ones.
Network destinations in shell commands (curl, scp, git push, publish) are extracted and logged.
Agent fetches cannot reach private, loopback, link-local or metadata addresses; DNS is resolved once and pinned, and redirects are re-checked.
Browser navigation and new tabs are limited to allowed domains and blocked from listed ones, with wildcard and scheme matching.
Each browser action is classified (read, mutating, navigation, egress) and allowed or denied by policy before it runs.
Electron window, navigation and IPC hardening
Links open only to safe schemes, privileged windows cannot navigate away, IPC checks the sender frame and media permissions are granted only to trusted frames.
Agent-made HTML, MCP apps and previews render in opaque-origin sandboxes with a CSP.
Rendered model output passes an allow-list sanitiser with safe URL schemes.
External images in model output load only when the user clicks, since URLs can leak data.
Web surfaces send CSP and security headers built per deployment.
Web pages, tool results, MCP output and imported text are wrapped as untrusted data; commands whose flags came from untrusted text get extra review.
Neutralise fake system tags and role headers
Fake <system> tags, [SYSTEM]: headers and confirmation-bypass phrases in user or outside text are escaped so they read as text.
Invisible tag characters, control and direction-override characters are stripped and text normalised to block hidden injections.
Inputs, context files, memory and cron prompts are scanned for injection, jailbreak and social-engineering patterns, then blocked, warned, filtered or rewritten.
Attacker-controlled MCP JSON schemas are bounded in bytes, depth and nodes before compiling or rewriting.
Inputs or outputs are checked against harm categories with thresholds (model or provider API).
Configured words or regexes block or mask content on the way in or out.
User-supplied regexes run with size and CPU-time caps to prevent ReDoS.
Messages, files, memories and tool arguments are scanned for personal data and blocked, redacted or pseudonymised, with an audit trail.
Secret redaction in logs, prompts and tool output
Secrets and codes are masked in logs, model prompts, tool results, traces and artifacts.
Secret masking in API and config responses
Settings and config sent to the UI mask keys and URL secrets, and masked placeholders are swapped back on save.
Secrets split across streamed chunks are still masked before deltas leave the process.
Named secrets injected by reference and masked by value
Secrets are referenced by name ($NAME), injected only into the command that needs them, and every value is masked wherever it appears afterwards.
Secret placeholders at the model boundary
The model only sees placeholders for secrets; real values are substituted at action time.
A stored credential is released only to the site it belongs to, with warnings when domains do not match.
Inject credentials at the network edge
Sandboxes, coding agents and WASM add-ons hold only dummy values; the real credential is swapped in at egress for matching destinations.
Spawned commands and servers get a filtered environment without credentials or code-injection variables, with explicit passthrough.
The binary disables core dumps and ptrace and strips preload variables at start.
Secrets are bound only to the skills that declare them and stripped from child processes afterwards.
Remote workers get rotating short-lived credentials instead of long-lived secrets.
Config names secrets by reference (env, file, command, Bitwarden, 1Password, store) and resolves them in memory instead of storing values.
A command finds plaintext credentials in config and env and migrates them into secret references.
OS keychain storage with encrypted fallback
Tokens live in the OS keychain; if unavailable, an encrypted file is used, never reversible encoding.
Secrets are encrypted at rest (AES-GCM, key in the OS keychain) with access scoping and audit.
Credential files are written atomically with owner-only permissions.
The local database can be encrypted with SQLCipher.
A settings page creates, edits and deletes named secrets with descriptions, injected into the agent without revealing values.
Per-provider forms collect API keys or subscription files and warn about conflicts.
The agent asks for a credential through a trusted prompt that stores it directly; the model never sees it.
Sign-ins fill from a vault or password manager (Bitwarden, 1Password) at fill time; the model sees only which login exists.
Password-manager broker with reason and audit
Agents get a curated list of secrets and must give a reason; each fetch follows an approval policy and is audited.
Mask typed secrets and password fields
Values typed into password fields are detected and masked in recordings, previews and the UI.
Chat media are stored as file-id references instead of URLs that embed the bot token.
Auth headers survive redirects only on the same origin.
All HTTP clients use the operating system's certificate verifier.
Loopback-only by default; key required when exposed
Local servers bind to 127.0.0.1; exposing them beyond loopback requires a key or token, and loopback trust cannot be faked with forwarded headers.
